source.title_on_document: Can large language models teach creativity? Cognitive gains, affective gaps, and distinct neural patterns

supplement.where: Appendix A. Supplementary data: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100288' (p. 12)
supplement.holds: Table S2, which the text cites for 'descriptive stats for all Means and SDs' at the end of the pre-test homogeneity paragraph (p. 5, Section 3); the paper does not say whether it includes post-test means and SDs by arm. Also Fig. S1 and Table S1 (fNIRS optode and channel positions, p. 5), Fig. S2 (current and future learning motivation, p. 7), the human instructors' scripts and the backup learning materials (p. 4), and all subjective-perception scales (p. 3). The main text prints means and SDs only for the AI arm's post-test scores; the human and control arms' levels appear only as Fig. 2 bars.

paper_design_summary: In a laboratory study with fNIRS recording, run by a Shanghai Normal University team, 95 right-handed adults recruited through university advertisements were randomly assigned to about 8-10 minutes of one-to-one creativity instruction from ChatGPT-4.0 (text chat that followed a standard guideline with example prompts), the same length of scripted, face-to-face heuristic instruction from a trained human instructor, or quiet rest with eyes closed. Everyone did an Alternative Uses Task before the instruction ('books') and three in a post-test phase after it ('books' again for acquisition; 'umbrellas' and 'can' for transfer), and two trained raters scored the responses for fluency, originality, and flexibility. Participants also rated affiliative bonding and interaction quality; these self-reports are not listed as outcomes.

studies.label: Lab experiment: ChatGPT-4.0 instruction vs human instruction vs rest control, AUT before and after, with fNIRS

assignment.what_was_assigned: Type of creativity instruction for one 8-10 min session: ChatGPT-4.0 as instructor, a trained human instructor following a standardized script, or no instruction (quiet rest). Instruction type is the between-subjects factor of the paper's 3 x 2 mixed design; time (pre-test vs post-test) is its within-subjects factor and is not an assigned condition. The randomization procedure is not described.
assignment.quote: They were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: AI (n = 31, 27 females), human (n = 34, 21 females), and control (n = 30, 28 females).
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 2.1 Participants; p. 4, Section 2.3 (3 x 2 mixed design: instruction type between subjects, time within subjects); p. 1, Abstract ('95 participants were randomized')

arms.name: AI instruction
arms.description: One-to-one, real-time text chat with ChatGPT-4.0 acting as creativity instructor for about 8-10 min. Beforehand every participant read the same brief guideline with example prompts ('teach me some strategies for creativity and divergent thinking, such as association or decomposition'; 'I'm thinking about different uses for books—how can I generate more novel ideas?'; 'Are there any more original ideas?'). Backup learning materials on association, decomposition, adaptation, and combination were provided. Researchers monitored the chat logs during the session.

arms.name: Human instruction
arms.description: Face-to-face, one-to-one heuristic, dialogue-based instruction from a postgraduate education student trained in lecturing, following a standardized script (association, decomposition, and combination strategies) reviewed by three professors; same duration. Instructors did not know their participants.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Sat quietly with eyes closed for the same duration, with no instruction or interaction.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper gives arm counts at assignment (31, 34, 30; total 95) and reports no exclusions or dropouts. The creativity ANOVAs report F(2,92) and Fs(1,92), which with three groups imply 95 people analyzed; the AI vs human t-tests report t(63) (31 + 34 = 65) and the AI-only one-sample t-tests t(30). The analyzed counts, in total and by arm, are derived from these degrees of freedom; the paper does not print them in words.
participants.who: Right-handed adults (76 females; mean age 21.82, SD 2.44) recruited through university advertisements, with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, one to two years of comparable experience with AI tools, and comparable educational backgrounds; paid about 40 yuan. Fig. 1A labels the learner 'Student' in all three condition panels; the Methods text does not call the participants students.
participants.country: China (ethics approval from Shanghai Normal University, 2025061; the participants' country is not stated in words)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4.0 (as printed on p. 4; 'ChatGPT 4.0' on p. 11; no model date)
ai_tool.how_used: ChatGPT served as a creativity instructor in a free, real-time dialogue during the 8-10 min instruction phase. The guideline's example prompts ask it to teach strategies and to give more novel or original ideas, including for 'books', the pre-test and acquisition item, so the AI could supply ideas as well as strategies. Researchers monitored the chat logs to keep the AI on the heuristic protocol. The AI interaction belongs to the instruction phase only; the scored post-test came after a 60-s rest (pp. 4-5, Sections 2.3-2.4; Fig. 1B).

task.description: Alternative Uses Task: list as many creative uses as possible for an everyday object in 3 min. Pre-test item 'books'. Post-test items 'books' (identical item, creativity acquisition) and 'umbrellas' and 'can' (novel items, creativity transfer), post-test order counterbalanced.
task.duration: Pre-test 3 min; instruction about 8-10 min; post-test block 10 min holding three AUT items of 3 min each; 60-s rests between phases (p. 3, Section 2.2; p. 4, Fig. 1B)

outcomes.name: AUT originality, identical item 'books' (creativity acquisition)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained independent raters (reliability established on pilot data) rated each idea on a 5-point originality scale (1 = not at all original, 5 = very original) after all responses were pooled and duplicates removed; originality ICC 0.903-0.962. The two raters' scores were averaged into each participant's score. The paper does not state how per-idea originality ratings are aggregated within a participant (p. 3, Section 2.2). Rater blinding to condition is not stated. Analysis: 3 (instruction type) x 2 (time) mixed ANOVA on the 'books' pre-test and post-test, with post hoc comparisons; change scores (post minus pre) enter the brain-behavior correlations.
outcomes.delay: Same session: the post-test followed the 8-10 min instruction phase after a 60-s rest (Fig. 1B)

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1: individual random assignment to ChatGPT-4.0 creativity instruction, human instruction, or quiet rest is explicit (p. 3, Section 2.1; p. 4, Section 2.3). Criterion 2: 95 people were randomized, with arm counts 31, 34, and 30 (p. 3, Section 2.1); the participant-level mixed ANOVAs report F(2,92), supporting 95 analyzed people across the three arms, above the 50-person threshold (pp. 5-6, Section 3.1). The analyzed counts are derived from the degrees of freedom, not separately printed completion counts, and no creativity-analysis exclusions are reported. Criterion 3: two trained independent raters scored participants' own AUT responses for fluency, originality, and flexibility and averaged their ratings into participant scores (p. 3, Section 2.2). The procedure and Fig. 1B support immediate after_ai outcomes; explicit confirmation that ChatGPT was unavailable during the post-test would settle question coding, without changing any eligibility criterion (pp. 4-5, Sections 2.3-2.4). Missing supplementary descriptives and scoring details do not prevent eligibility.

one_line_finding: After 8-10 minutes of ChatGPT-4.0 instruction, post-test AUT originality and flexibility on the trained item and flexibility on new items were higher than after human instruction or quiet rest (e.g., novel-item flexibility AI 9.67 ± 3.40, interaction F(2,92) = 7.182, p = 0.001; AI vs human p = 0.002, AI vs control p < 0.001), while no AI-versus-comparator post-test fluency difference is reported (pp. 5-6, Section 3.1; p. 6, Fig. 2).
open_questions: The text prints the AI group's post-test flexibility on the identical item as 7.29 ± 2.97 (p. 5), but Fig. 2C draws the AI post-test bar near 10 and the AI pre-test bar near 7 with an error bar of about 3; the same pre-test bar in Fig. 2F also sits near 7. The printed value may be the pre-test mean. The form records it as printed; Table S2 (not on file) may settle it.

Human and control arm levels appear only as Fig. 2 bars. The one sentence that cites Table S2 (p. 5) says it holds 'descriptive stats for all Means and SDs' without saying whether post-test values by arm are included; the supplement is not on file.

The paper does not say in words that ChatGPT was unavailable during the post-test. The procedure places the AI interaction in the instruction phase only, followed by a 60-s rest and the post-test (pp. 4-5, Section 2.4; Fig. 1B), so ai_available_when_produced is coded no.

The AI guideline's example prompt asks about 'different uses for books', the item of the pre-test and the acquisition post-test, and the paper says instruction builds on learners' inputs such as 'book' (p. 3). Identical-item outcomes may partly reflect recall of ideas from the instruction session.

The paper states that two raters scored each idea and that their ratings were averaged to yield each participant's score, but it does not specify how originality ratings for multiple ideas are aggregated within a participant (p. 3, Section 2.2). The aggregation rule needs confirmation from the authors; no sum or mean across ideas is assumed.
The paper does not state how scores on the two novel items ('umbrellas', 'can') combine into the transfer scores.

Fig. 2E annotates AI post vs control post p = 0.0230 on novel-item originality, while the text reports a non-significant interaction (p = 0.139) and instruction main effect (ps ≥ 0.144) and does not mention the pairwise comparison.
Population coded students from the university-advertisement recruitment and the 'Student' labels in Fig. 1A; the text does not state that all participants were enrolled students.

AI role coded open_chat. A case exists for coach, because ChatGPT acted as an instructor teaching strategies, but participants could ask it for ideas, and the guideline's example prompts ask for 'more original ideas'.
The AI vs human contrast confounds the instructor with the medium (text chat vs face-to-face), as the authors note (p. 11, Section 4.4).
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on creative output: self-reported affiliative bonding, interaction quality, perceived usefulness, ease of use, and learning intentions (Section 3.2, pp. 6-7; Fig. 3, p. 7; Supplementary Fig. S2); fNIRS activation and functional connectivity (Sections 3.3-3.4, p. 7; Figs. 4-5, pp. 8-9); and brain-behavior correlations (Section 3.5, pp. 7-8; Fig. 6, p. 10). Pre-test equivalence: fluency F(2,92) = 0.09, p = 0.913; flexibility F(2,92) = 0.34, p = 0.710; originality F(2,92) = 0.47, p = 0.626 (p. 5, Section 3). Main effects of time: identical items Fs(1,92) ≥ 48.94, ps < 0.001; novel items Fs(1,92) ≥ 5.78, ps < 0.018 (pp. 5-6). Human vs control post-tests did not differ on identical items (ps ≥ 0.314) or novel items (p. 6). The a priori power analysis targeted at least 66 participants (p. 3). Outcome numbering follows B; A numbered novel-item flexibility S1-O4 and novel-item originality S1-O5. The reconciliation corrected two fields on which both screeners agreed: assignment.structure (mixed to between) and statistics_available for the five contrasts with no pairwise p-value (see reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked). Final review covered the entire saved markdown, including Appendix A and references, and checked the relevant PDF text and embedded Figs. 1-2. All three challenge files (assignment, outcome, people) contain no problems, so challenge_resolution is empty and its action counts are zero. The originality aggregation rule remains unstated; the suggestion that it was a sum has been removed. Appendix A links a separate supplement; urllib requests to the printed DOI and the ScienceDirect URL named in retrieval.json both failed with WinError 10013, so Table S2 was not inspected. No missing supplementary numbers or replacement values for the printed flexibility mean were supplied.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: The printed AI post-test flexibility for the identical item (7.29 ± 2.97, p. 5, Section 3.1) conflicts with the relative pre/post bar heights in Fig. 2C (p. 6). Retain the printed value; Table S2 should be checked for explicit post-test descriptives, with author clarification needed if it does not settle the discrepancy. This affects the outcome level, not eligibility.

open_questions[1]: Exact human and control arm means and SDs are not printed in the main text; the saved PDF shows them only as bars with SD error bars (pp. 5-6, Section 3.1 and Fig. 2). The separate supplement is needed to establish whether usable arm descriptives are available. This affects quantitative extraction, not eligibility.

open_questions[2]: The instruction/post-test sequence supports after_ai, but the article does not explicitly say ChatGPT was unavailable during the post-test (pp. 4-5, Sections 2.3-2.4; p. 4, Fig. 1B). Authors could confirm post-test access. This distinguishes after_ai from with_ai; either timing still satisfies the three eligibility criteria.

open_questions[3]: Books is explicitly both an instructional example and the repeated acquisition test item (p. 3, Section 2.2; p. 4, Section 2.3). Retain possible recall of instructional ideas as an interpretation limitation; no further information is needed for screening, and the novel-item transfer outcomes remain separately coded.

open_questions[4]: The rule for aggregating originality ratings across a participant's ideas is unstated; averaging the two raters does not specify this separate aggregation (p. 3, Section 2.2). Authors could supply the scoring rule. This affects score interpretation, while the scores are clearly based on produced output.

open_questions[5]: How the umbrellas and can post-test scores combine into the transfer outcome is unstated (p. 3, Section 2.2; pp. 5-6, Section 3.1). Authors could supply the aggregation rule. Both items are scored participant output, so the omission does not affect eligibility.

open_questions[6]: Fig. 2E explicitly annotates the AI-versus-control post-test originality comparison at p = 0.0230, while Section 3.1 reports a nonsignificant interaction and instruction main effect (p. 6). These are different tests; retain both the pairwise finding and the omnibus results as printed. No further information is needed to code the reported contrast or determine eligibility.

open_questions[7]: University advertisements and Fig. 1A's Student labels support the students code, but enrollment of every participant is not explicitly stated (p. 3, Section 2.1; p. 4, Fig. 1A). Authors could confirm the population. Student status is not an eligibility criterion.

open_questions[8]: open_chat is supported by real-time, participant-directed questions and follow-ups, including the example 'Are there any more original ideas?' (p. 4, Section 2.3). The codebook's coach role requires no supplied content, so no further information is needed to retain open_chat or generative-AI eligibility.

open_questions[9]: Text chat versus face-to-face instruction confounds communication medium with instructor type, as the authors explicitly acknowledge (p. 11, Section 4.4). This is a documented limitation of causal interpretation, not an unresolved assignment or outcome fact; no additional source is needed for screening.

Unresolved reconciliation.differences entry source.supplement.holds: the Table S2 citation promises descriptive means and SDs but occurs in the pre-test homogeneity paragraph and does not establish whether post-test arm descriptives are included (p. 5, Section 3; p. 12, Appendix A). Inspecting the separate supplement would settle its contents. The historical reconciliation remains unchanged; this omission affects extraction, not eligibility.
